topic: The iPad Slump vs iPhone Surge
description: Timeline comparison of Apple’s biggest handhelds: how iPhone growth (and Services) pulled ahead while iPad shipments fell from their peak after 2019—setting up a chart-race of market share, not vibes.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The iPad Slump vs iPhone Surge… and Services quietly won.

For years, Apple treated iPad like the steady second act: big screens, schools, creators, everyday productivity. But once the iPhone became the money printer—and Services grew into the long game—iPad stopped behaving like a guaranteed upward line.

In 2016, iPhone revenue sat at about $215.3B. iPad was only $18.0B—already smaller, but still relevant. Through 2017 and 2018, iPhone hovered in the $218–$230B range, while iPad bounced around a narrower band ($15.9B to $20.2B). By 2019 the contrast was sharper: iPhone dipped to $202.9B while iPad landed at $19.4B—no collapse yet, but momentum wasn’t building.

Then 2020 hits. iPhone revenue jumps to $274.5B, driven by iPhone demand and broader Apple ecosystem pull. iPad rises too—to about $24.0B—so the chart race looks briefly “balanced.” But by 2021, the script flips: iPhone rockets to $365.8B while iPad climbs more modestly to $28.3B. The gap becomes a canyon.

From 2022 to 2025, iPhone keeps extending the lead ($394.3B → $383.3B → $377.8B → $399.0B). iPad, meanwhile, peaks around 2022 ($31.2B) and cools afterward ($26.4B in 2023, $22.9B in 2024, then a partial recovery to ~$24.5B in 2025). And the plot twist? Services surges from $53.8B (2019) to $108.0B (2025), while Wearables grows from $13.7B (2019) to $47.5B (2025).

📉 So here’s the question for the comments: Do you think iPad’s slowdown is mostly product-cycle timing—or a real shift in how people use tablets now?

facebook_caption:
Apple’s handheld story from 2016–2025 is less about a single device and more about revenue gravity. iPhone revenue rose from about $215.3B (2016) to $399.0B (2025), with a major acceleration during 2020–2022 (from $274.5B in 2020 to $394.3B in 2022). In contrast, iPad revenue peaked earlier and then softened: after moving from $18.0B (2016) to roughly $31.2B (2022), iPad declined to $26.4B (2023) and $22.9B (2024), with only a partial rebound in 2025 (~$24.5B).

Two additional lines explain why Apple’s overall trajectory remained resilient. Services grew from $53.8B (2019) to $108.0B (2025), helping offset hardware fluctuations. Wearables, Home & Accessories also expanded from $13.7B (2019) to $47.5B (2025), showing that Apple’s growth increasingly came from the ecosystem—not just one product category.

In this timeline comparison, the chart race is clear: iPhone and Services pulled ahead, while iPad faced a post-peak cooldown.
